source.title: Five open problems in theory of quantum information

accepted.question_text: For an N-dimensional complex Hilbert space H_N, construct symmetric informationally complete positive-operator-valued measurements (SIC POVMs) in an infinite sequence of dimensions N_1, N_2, N_3, .... Concretely, for each dimension N in the sequence, find N^2 vectors |ψ_j⟩ in H_N whose squared overlaps satisfy |⟨ψ_j|ψ_k⟩|^2 = (N δ_jk + 1)/(N + 1) for all j,k = 1,...,N^2, so that the associated projectors form a simplex in the N^2−1 dimensional set of density matrices.

evidence.quote: Problem 1: Construct SIC POVMs in an infinite sequence of dimensions,N1, N2, N3, . . . Setup. A symmetric informationally complete positive operator valued measure [15, 16] associated with an N-dimensional complex Hilbert spaceHN is given by a set ofN2 vectors∣ψj⟩∈ HN satisfying the following overlap relations, ∣⟨ψj∣ψk⟩∣2= N δjk+ 1 N+ 1 , j, k = 1, . . . , N2.

However, in spite of a considerable research effort [27–31], the general conjecture of Zauner remains unproven. Finding a family of SICs in any infinite sequence of dimensions could become a decisive step in this direction.

accepted.question_text: For complex Hilbert-space dimensions N that are not prime powers, determine how many mutually unbiased bases can exist. Here a set of bases in H_N is mutually unbiased when each basis is orthonormal and, for any two different bases, every squared overlap between one vector from each basis equals 1/N; no more than N+1 such bases can exist, prime-power dimensions achieve N+1, and the non-prime-power case remains unresolved.
accepted.context_brief: Maximum number of MUBs outside prime-power dimensions

evidence.quote: These bases are called mutually unbiased if any two bases are unbiased, which means ∀i,j ∣⟨ψm i ∣ψn j ⟩∣2= 1 N , m ≠ n. (2) It is relatively easy to show that there exist no more than N + 1 MUBs in HN.
If N is a power of a prime, various properties of a complete set ofN+1 MUBs are already understood [43–47], but otherwise the number of existing MUBs remains unknown [48–50].

accepted.question_text: In the six-dimensional complex Hilbert space H_6, either construct a set of at least four mutually unbiased bases or prove that a complete set of seven mutually unbiased bases does not exist. A mutually unbiased-basis set consists of orthonormal bases such that vectors from distinct bases have squared inner product 1/6; the general upper bound in dimension 6 is seven bases, but only triples are currently known in the cited literature.

evidence.quote: Problem 2: Construct a set of at least 4 mutually unbiased bases in dimension six or prove that there are no 7 MUBs in H6.
In particular, for N = 6 a complete set would consist of seven MUBs, but up till now only solutions containing three bases were found [51–60].
There exist 4, 5, and 6 MUBs in dimensionsN = 3, 4 and 5, respectively. How many MUBs there exist forN = 6?

accepted.question_text: Determine whether two quantum orthogonal Latin squares of order 6 exist. Equivalently, decide whether the classical 36 officers obstruction can be overcome by replacing the officers or cards with quantum states in H_6⊗H_6 arranged as a 6×6 table of 36 mutually orthogonal normalized vectors whose row and column superpositions are maximally entangled; a negative decision is equivalent to proving that there is no absolutely maximally entangled state of four six-level subsystems, no ((4,1,3))_6 quantum error-correction code, no 2-unitary matrix in U(36), and no perfect tensor with four indices each running from 1 to 6.
accepted.context_brief: Quantum orthogonal Latin squares of order six

evidence.quote: Problem 3: Determine whether there exist two quantum orthogonal Latin squares [77, 78] of order six. In other words, find a solution of the problem of 36 ‘entangled officers’ of Euler or demonstrate that it does not exist.

Orthogonal quantum Latin squares(OQLS) are defined [77] as a collection of N2 normalized vectors from a composite spaceHN⊗HN, which are mutually orthogonal so they form an orthonormal basis. They are arranged in anN×N table such that for every row (column) the symmetric superposition of all states in each row (column) is a maximally entangled state.

As there are no two orthogonal Latin squares (OLS) of order six, the famous classical problem of36 officers of Euler has no solution [100]. An analogous quantum problem, which involves 36 entangled officers, remains open.

Establishing a negative result concerning existence of two quantum orthogonal Latin squares of order six is equivalent to proving that i) there is no AME state of four subsystems with six levels each [97, 103] thus the corresponding quantum error correction code [104], written((4, 1, 3))6, does not exist; ii) there is no 2-unitary matrixU ∈ U(36); iii) there is no perfect tensor with four indices, each running from 1 to 6.

accepted.question_text: For an arbitrary order N, determine the maximal possible number of mutually orthogonal Latin squares. A Latin square of order N is an N×N array using N copies of N symbols with no repeated symbol in any row or column, and a set of mutually orthogonal Latin squares consists of Latin squares whose pairwise ordered symbol pairs occur exactly once; at most N−1 such squares can exist, prime-power orders attain this bound, but the general maximum remains open.
accepted.context_brief: Maximum number of MOLS for arbitrary order

evidence.quote: A Latin square of order N is filled with N copies of N symbols arranged in a square in such a way that no row nor column of the square contains the same symbol twice.

A set ofk Latin squares which are pairwise orthogonal are called mutually orthogonal Latin squares(MOLS). It is easy to show that for a givenN there exist no more thanN− 1 MOLSs. Similarly with the case of the MUBs, this bound is saturated ifN is a prime or a power of a prime [80].
In general, the problem of finding the maximal number of MOLS for an arbitrary value ofN remains open [83].

accepted.question_text: Explain whether the behavior of mutually unbiased measurements in coarse-grained or continuous-variable quantum systems is connected to the unresolved special role of discrete Hilbert-space dimension N=6. Continuous systems have at most three mutually unbiased bases, coarse-grained even-dimensional systems behave like continuous systems with no more than three mutually unbiased measurements, and it remains open whether this is related to the dimension-6 conundrum for discrete systems.

evidence.quote: While in the continuous case we maximally have3 MUBs [106], in the coarse-grained scenario [108] the situation is much more elaborate. Interestingly, the special dimension N = 6is not at all distinguished in the coarse-grained setting, since the systems of even dimension behave like the continuous ones (no more than 3 MUMs) — only odd dimensions nurture potential for more [108]. Whether this fact is connected to the conundrum ofN = 6 for discrete systems remains and open question at the moment.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether bound entangled states with negative partial transpose exist. In self-contained terms: decide whether there are bipartite quantum states that are entangled but nondistillable, while the partial transpose of the density matrix has at least one strictly negative eigenvalue; an equivalent Werner-state formulation asks whether there exists a negative-partial-transpose Werner state that is nondistillable for local dimension d>2.

evidence.quote: Problem 4: Establish whether there exist bound entangled states with negative partial transpose.

A quantum state is said to havepositive partial transpose (PPT)ifalleigenvaluesofitspartialtransposearenonegative. Otherwise, if some eigenvalues of ρΓ are strictly smaller than zero, the state has negative partial transpose (NPT).

However, in higher dimensional systems some entangled states can be distilled to a singlet form [127], but there exist also nondistillable entangled states, which are called bound entangled[128, 129].
This theorem implies that the current, fourth problem canbeformulatedasfollows: Decide, whether there exists an NPT Werner state which is nondistillable.

accepted.question_text: For Werner states ρ(d,α) on H_d⊗H_d, determine whether every Werner state that is not 1-copy distillable is nondistillable for all finite numbers of copies. Using the parameterization ρ(d,α) = (I⊗I + αV)/(d^2 + αd), where V is the swap operator, the conjecture says that 1-copy nondistillability should coincide with complete nondistillability for this family.

evidence.quote: Consider the family of Werner states defined on the Hilbert spaceHd⊗ Hd as ρ(d, α)= 1 l⊗ 1 l+ αV d2+ αd , (5) with the general range of the parameter α ∈ [−1, 1]. The matrix V stands for the Swap operator, defined by its matrix elements, ⟨ij∣V∣kl⟩ = δilδjk.
It was conjectured [133–136, 141] that the Werner states which are not 1-copy distillable are just not-distillable, so in particular they are also2-copy non-distillable.
A stronger conjecture that for Werner states 1-copy nondistillability is equivalent to complete non-distillability, means that B∞= B1 in Fig. 5.

accepted.question_text: Show that the two-ququart Werner state ρ(4,−1/2) is not 2-copy distillable. Equivalently, prove that for every Kronecker sum A⊕B = A⊗I + I⊗B with traceless 4×4 matrices A and B satisfying Tr(A†A)+Tr(B†B)=1/4, the sum of squares of the two largest singular values is at most 1/2.

evidence.quote: Problem 5: Show that the Werner stateρ(4,−1/2) of two ququarts,d = 4, defined in Eq. (5) below, is not 2-copy distillable.

A distinguished state of this family,ρ(4,−1/2), appearing in the problem considered here, is the only two-ququart Werner state such that its partial transpose (see Eq. 4) is proportional to a unitary matrix.

Interestingly, thisquestionisalso equivalent to the following algebraic problem [134]: Show that the sum of squares of the two largest singular values is bounded by1/2 for any Kronecker (tensor) sum, A⊕ B= A⊗ 1 l+ 1 l⊗ B, where A and B denote traceless matrices of size4 satisfying Tr(A†A)+ Tr(B†B)= 1/4.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether all negative-partial-transpose entangled states represent quantum privacy that can be distilled to private bit states, and, if the answer is positive, determine whether such private-bit distillation can be achieved with one-way classical communication from one party to the other. Here negative partial transpose means the partial transpose of the bipartite density matrix has a strictly negative eigenvalue, and private bit states are the target privacy resource.

evidence.quote: Otherwise, if some eigenvalues of ρΓ are strictly smaller than zero, the state has negative partial transpose (NPT).

Problem 4 seems to be rather complex, so its solution may involve some novel techniques concerning tensor products of several matrices. Its positive solution would likely stimulate research on an important question relevant for quantum communication, namely, whether all NPT entangled states represent quantum privacy that may be distilled to the so-called private bit states – see [144]. If the answer were positive, the practical question would be, whether such a distillation procedure can be achieved in the scheme called ‘one-way classical communication’, in which one party, say Alice, communicates classical bits to Bob, and not vice versa.

needs_review.question_text_raw: What are the most entangled states for quantum systems consisting of N systems with d levels each ?

evidence.quote: For other systems, a natural question arises [87–96]: What are the most entangled states for quantum systems consisting of N systems with d levels each ? The answer depends on the entanglement measure used [19], but already for a four-qutrit system there exist a state, which displays maximal entanglement with respect to all three possible splittings of the entire system into two pairs of qutrits.
